name: Shan states
summary: Dozens of Tai-speaking principalities ruled by saophas in the hills of eastern Burma; often under Burmese overlords and later British rule, they joined independent Burma in 1948.

location.value: The Shan plateau of eastern Myanmar, between the Irrawaddy valley, Yunnan (China), Laos and Thailand.

terrain.value: A high plateau (about 1,000 m) cut by the Salween River, with valleys, lakes such as Inle and steep hills.

climate.value: Cooler than lowland Burma, with a monsoon rainy season and dry winters.

resources.value: Rice in the valleys, tea, teak forests and silver and lead at Bawdwin.

disasters.value: Floods, landslides and wars that burned towns.

population.value: Perhaps 1–1.5 million in the 1800s, many of them hill peoples rather than Shan.

urbanisation.value: Small walled princely capitals such as Hsipaw, Kengtung, Yawnghwe and Hsenwi.

migration.value: Tai-speaking Shan settled the valleys after about 1200; Kachin, Palaung, Wa and other peoples lived in the hills.

economicBase.value: Wet-rice farming in valleys, tea and forest products in the hills.

tradeRoutes.value: Mule caravans linked Burma with Yunnan and northern Thailand.

wealth.value: Modest; princes taxed rice and caravans.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver, rice and tribute paid to the saopha and to the Burmese king.

inequality.value: Princely families (saophas) and officials above farmers; hill peoples were often subordinate.

governmentType.value: About 30–40 principalities, each under a hereditary saopha (“lord of the sky”).

keyRulers.value: Saophas of Mong Mao, Hsenwi and Kengtung; Sao Shwe Thaik of Yawnghwe (first president of Burma, 1948).

succession.value: Hereditary within princely families, confirmed by the Burmese king or later the British.

institutions.value: Princely courts with ministers; Buddhist monasteries.

stability.value: Frequent wars between principalities and with Burmese kings.

armyAndTech.value: Infantry and cavalry levies; later muskets.

majorWars.value: The Shan Confederation defeated Ava in 1527; Bayinnaung captured Ava in 1555 and conquered all the Shan States in 1556–57.

territoryChange.value: Under Toungoo and Konbaung Burma; British protectorate from 1887; Federated Shan States (1922).

alliancesRivals.value: Burmese kings, Chinese frontier officials and Lan Na.

inventions.value: No major inventions; Shan paper (from mulberry bark) and lacquerware.

scienceEducation.value: Monastery schools taught reading and Buddhist texts.

openness.value: Open to caravan trade with China and Siam.

communicationTransport.value: Mule and pony caravans; boats on Inle Lake.

languageWriting.value: Shan (a Tai language) in its own script.

socialStructure.value: Princes, officials, monks, farmers; hill peoples.

sharedIdentity.value: A Tai (Shan) identity distinct from the Burmese.

dailyLife.value: Rice, Shan noodles, tea; houses on stilts.

neighbours.value: Burma, Yunnan (China), Lan Na, Lao kingdoms.

ideasReligions.value: Buddhist kingship shared with Burma and Siam.

colonisation.value: By 1885 the British occupied all of present-day Myanmar; the states became princely states under British paramountcy and were federated in 1922.

riseSignals.value: Möng Mao arose in the power vacuum left by the fall of the Kingdom of Dali (about 1254) and ended the kingdoms of Sagaing and Pinya in 1364.

outcome.value: The saophas’ hereditary rights were removed by General Ne Win’s government in 1962; the infobox says the states were fully annexed in 1959, so the dates conflict.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are well documented; population figures are estimates.
